script: Good morning, this is Stocksplain for Monday, November 23. Markets are feeling the whiplash after a massive global tech sell-off wiped out about nine trillion dollars in S&P five hundred value since early October. The Nasdaq has officially entered correction territory, dropping about thirteen percent from its peak, while semiconductor indexes plunged over forty percent. The turbulence reflects cooling enthusiasm for high-flying artificial intelligence stocks, tight dollar funding liquidity, and heavy corporate stock issuances that have absorbed billions of investor dollars. Asian regulators have even launched emergency stabilization measures as international indexes take a hit. In other major tech news, Nvidia experienced a dramatic roller coaster. The company's stock jumped twenty-seven percent and added about eight hundred forty billion dollars in a single day after its board reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as chief executive officer following consultations with senior government officials. That sharp reversal came on the heels of a steep thirty-two percent year-to-date drop fueled by leadership uncertainty, export control fears, and governance concerns. Meanwhile, the gaming industry is grappling with soaring production costs. Grand Theft Auto VI finally launched after a thirteen-year wait, highlighting an era where only a tiny handful of publishers with massive cash-cow franchises can absorb the immense financial risk of building multi-year blockbusters. As mega-budget projects become unsustainable for smaller studios, developers are increasingly turning to digital distribution and lower-cost creation engines to stay afloat. Today we are explaining a correction. A correction happens when a stock, index, or asset price falls between ten and twenty percent from its recent peak. While corrections can feel alarming, they are a normal part of market cycles and often serve to cool down overvalued sectors. Thank you for listening, and have a great trading day.
